bib.title: Billion-scale similarity search with GPUs
bib.venue: preprint (arXiv:1702.08734v1 [cs.CV], 28 Feb 2017); published as IEEE Trans. Big Data 2021

question: How can similarity search (exact, IVFADC product-quantization, k-NN graph building) be made to use GPUs near peak throughput at billion-vector scale?
hypothesis: Prior GPU approaches are bottlenecked by k-min selection and poor memory-hierarchy use; a register-resident k-selection fused with distance kernels removes this.
contributions: a GPU k-selection algorithm, operating in fast register memory and flexible enough to be fusable with other kernels, for which we provide a complexity analysis
a near-optimal algorithmic layout for exact and approximate k-nearest neighbor search on GPU
a range of experiments that show that these improvements outperform previous art by a large margin on mid- to large-scale nearest-neighbor search tasks, in single or multi-GPU configurations

method.summary: WarpSelect keeps k-selection state in GPU registers using odd-size merge/sort networks, fused with a cuBLAS GEMM-based L2 distance kernel for exact search. IVFADC (coarse k-means quantizer plus product quantizer on residuals) is implemented with PQ lookup tables in shared memory, multi-pass k-selection, and replication/sharding over GPUs. Evaluated on k-selection, k-means, exact and billion-scale approximate search, and k-NN graph construction.
method.task: k-nearest-neighbour search under L2 distance on GPUs

datasets.name: YFCC100M subset
datasets.split: 10,000 sampled images with exact neighbours for quality
datasets.preprocessing: one-before-last layer of a ResNet, PCA to d=128

models.name: WarpSelect + IVFADC GPU implementation (Faiss)
models.architecture: IVFADC: |C1|~sqrt(l) coarse centroids by k-means; PQ with 256 centroids per sub-quantizer; b a multiple of 4 up to 64 in GPU implementation

inference.samples: not stated: single timing runs reported, no repeats or variance
inference.retrieval: IVFADC multi-probe tau from 1 to 256 in graph experiments; Sift1B m=8 bytes; Deep1B m=20, |C1|=2^18, d=80 via OPQ; YFCC100M |C1|=2^16 and m=16,32,64; Deep1B graph |C1|=2^18, m=20,40, d=120; k-selection k<=1024

parameters.multi-GPU: Deep1B S=2,R=2; YFCC100M S=1,R=4; also 8 Maxwell M40
parameters.k-selection benchmark: nq=10000, k=100 and 1000, l from 1000 to 128000, 32-bit floats

other.hardware: 2x2.8GHz Intel Xeon E5-2680v2 with 4 Maxwell Titan X GPUs, CUDA 8.0
other.limits_on_b: b limited to at most 48 (fp32) or 96 (fp16) by shared memory for lookup tables

metrics.name: R@1 / R@10 / R@100
metrics.definition: fraction of queries where the true nearest neighbor is in the top 1 (resp. 10, 100) results

metrics.name: k-NN graph accuracy
metrics.definition: fraction of the 10 found nearest neighbors within the ground-truth 10 nearest neighbors, on 10,000 sampled images

metrics.name: fraction of peak
metrics.definition: measured throughput vs memory-bandwidth limit of the Titan X

baselines: Babenko and Lempitsky 2016 CPU result on Deep1B
eval.protocol: Single timing per configuration; Wieschollek and Deep1B CPU numbers are as reported by their authors, on different hardware. No seeds or variance.

results.claim: On SIFT1B with 8-byte codes, recall R@10 is 0.376 at 17.7 us per query on one GPU.
results.setup: Sift1B (1 billion SIFT features), nq=10^4 queries, 1 Maxwell Titan X GPU, IVFADC with m=8 bytes per vector; baseline is Wieschollek et al. as reported, matched on memory
results.quote: R@10 = 0.376 in 17.7 µs per query vector

results.claim: Same SIFT1B setting: 8.5x faster than Wieschollek et al. at higher recall.
results.setup: Sift1B (1 billion SIFT features), nq=10^4 queries, 1 Maxwell Titan X GPU, IVFADC with m=8 bytes per vector; baseline is Wieschollek et al. as reported, matched on memory
results.note: Abstract states '8.5× faster than prior GPU state of the art'; 150/17.7 = 8.5.
results.quote: more accurate at a speed 8.5× faster

results.claim: On SIFT1M at the same time budget (0.02 ms per query, Titan X), R@1 is 0.80 vs 0.51 for Wieschollek et al.
results.setup: Sift1M, Titan X, 0.02 ms per query; R@1 = fraction of queries whose true NN is in the top 1
results.quote: our implementation obtains R@1 = 0.80 and R@100 = 0.95

results.claim: On Deep1B, IVFADC on 4 GPUs reaches R@1 0.4517 in 0.0133 ms per vector, vs a CPU result of 0.45 in 20 ms.
results.setup: Deep1B (1B CNN vectors), nq=10^4, PQ m=20 with d=80 via OPQ, |C1|=2^18, 20 GB, 4 GPUs with S=2, R=2; CPU baseline is 1 thread from the dataset paper, different hardware
results.quote: We obtain a R@1 = 0.4517 in 0.0133 ms per vector

results.claim: WarpSelect runs at 55% of peak memory-bandwidth performance at k=100 but 16% at k=1000.
results.setup: k-selection on random 32-bit floats, nq=10000 arrays, l=128000, one Titan X
results.quote: WarpSelect operates at 55% of peak at k = 100 but only 16% of peak at k = 1000

results.claim: WarpSelect is 1.62x faster than the best compared k-selection at k=100 and 2.01x at k=1000.
results.setup: l=128000, nq=10000, Titan X; compared with fgknn (Tang et al.) and TBiS (Sismanis et al.)
results.note: Text says 'relative performance of WarpSelect over fgknn', so the baseline is fgknn.
results.quote: WarpSelect is 1.62× faster at k = 100, 2.01× at k = 1000

results.claim: Exact k-means on MNIST8m (256 centroids, 20 iterations) takes 140 s on one GPU vs 320 s for BIDMach.
results.setup: MNIST8m, 8.1M x 784-d, 20 iterations, 1 Titan X; 4 GPUs: 84 s (256) and 100 s (4096 centroids)
results.table: Table 1, row Ours 1 GPU, column 256 centroids

results.claim: Replicating over 4 GPUs gives 3.16x speedup for k-means with 4096 centroids.
Exact search on SIFT1M reaches 85% of peak possible performance; removing the fused L2/k-selection kernel is at least 25% slower.
results.setup: SIFT1M, l=10^6, d=128, nq=10^4, 1 Titan X, varying k
results.note: The 25% slowdown without fusion is stated as 'at least 25% slower'.
results.quote: which has 85 % of the peak possible

results.claim: A k-NN graph (k=10) on 95M YFCC100M images with accuracy above 0.8 is built in 35 minutes on 4 Titan X GPUs.
results.setup: YFCC100M 95M images, ResNet descriptors PCA to d=128, |C1|=2^16, S=1 R=4; end-to-end including index build; accuracy = fraction of 10 found NN within true 10 NN on 10,000 sampled images
results.quote: An accuracy of more than 0.8 is obtained in 35 minutes

results.claim: A Deep1B k-NN graph takes about 6 hours at lower quality and about half a day at higher quality.
results.setup: Deep1B, d=120 via OPQ, |C1|=2^18, m=20 or 40, 4 GPUs
results.quote: a lower-quality graph can be built in 6 hours

results.claim: Exact k-means of 10^8 128-d vectors to 85k centroids takes 52 minutes on 4 GPUs, against 46 min plus at least 56 min preprocessing for an approximate CPU method.
results.quote: Our method performs exact k-means on 4 GPUs in 52 minutes

results.claim: Fused distance-and-scan kernel for IVFADC improves timing by at most 15%, so the authors do not use it.
results.quote: Timing for the fused kernel is improved by at most 15%

results.claim: Thread queue length t is chosen by experiment: t=2 for k<=32, 3 for k<=128, 4 for k<=256, 8 for k<=1024.
Rule of thumb: number of coarse centroids |C1| is about sqrt(l), trained by k-means.

limits: Compared numbers for Wieschollek et al. and the Deep1B CPU baseline are taken from those papers' reports, on different hardware.
No variance, repeats or seeds are reported.
Only exact search and IVFADC are covered; graph indexes, filtering, updates and deletes are not tested.
Authors concede GWarpSelect efficiency drops at large k (16% of peak at k=1000) and that the k-means benchmark is somewhat unrealistic.
The PDF is the arXiv v1 text (2017), not the 2021 journal version; Maxwell-era GPUs and CUDA 8 are dated.
IVFADC parameters for Sift1B (|C1|, tau) are not stated.
